items.title: A truth table
items.prose: Fill the truth table of $P \Rightarrow (Q \Rightarrow P)$. Work out the inner implication first.
items.question: Fill in both columns with T or F.

feedback.correct: Every row is T: the statement is a tautology.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An implication is F only when its hypothesis is T and its conclusion F.

byKey.r1c2: On the T, F row the hypothesis $Q$ is F, so $Q \Rightarrow P$ is T.
byKey.r2c2: On the F, T row $Q$ is T and $P$ is F, so $Q \Rightarrow P$ is F.
byKey.r2c3: On the F, T row the outer hypothesis $P$ is F, so the whole implication is T.
byKey.r3c3: On the F, F row the outer hypothesis $P$ is F, so the whole is T.

explain.text: When $P$ is T, $Q \Rightarrow P$ has a true conclusion, so it is T. When $P$ is F, the outer implication is vacuously T. So every row is T: a tautology.

items.title: Words to symbols
items.prose: Let $P$ be “the price is above £100”, $Q$ “volume is above 1 million” and $R$ “the alert fires”. The rule: **if the price is above £100 and volume is not above 1 million, the alert does not fire**.
items.question: Which is the rule in symbols?

options.why: You swapped the hypothesis and the conclusion. The “if” part comes first.
That is the negation of a different rule. The sentence negates $Q$ and $R$ only.
You turned **and** into **or**. Both conditions must hold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Translate the “if” part, then the “then” part.

explain.text: The “if” part is “$P$ and not $Q$”, so the hypothesis is $P \land \lnot Q$. The conclusion is “not $R$”. The rule is $(P \land \lnot Q) \Rightarrow \lnot R$.

items.title: Three quantifiers
items.prose: Claim: **for every desk there is a day on which every trader on that desk made a profit**.

state.caption: Desk A: traders A1 and A2. Desk B: traders B1 and B2.

items.question: Show the claim is true: for each desk, tap its witness day for both of its traders.

feedback.correct: Desk A on Wednesday and desk B on Tuesday.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each desk, find a column where both of its traders are positive.

byKey.one-day: You used Tuesday for both desks. A1 lost £10 on Tuesday, so desk A needs another day.
byKey.r1c1: A2 lost £20 on Monday, so Monday fails for desk A.
byKey.r3c3: B1 lost £30 on Wednesday, so Wednesday fails for desk B.

explain.text: The claim is $\forall k\ \exists d\ \forall t$: each desk gets its own day. Desk A's both traders profit only on Wednesday, desk B's only on Tuesday.

items.title: Moving the quantifiers
items.prose: Same table. $k$ is a desk, $d$ a day and $t$ a trader on desk $k$. $P(k, d, t)$ says that trader made a profit that day.

state.caption: Desk A: traders A1 and A2. Desk B: traders B1 and B2.

items.question: Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\forall k\ \exists d\ \forall t\ P(k, d, t)$
$\exists d\ \forall k\ \forall t\ P(k, d, t)$
options.why: You need one column of four profits. Every column has a loss.

options.text: $\forall k\ \forall d\ \exists t\ P(k, d, t)$
$\forall k\ \exists t\ \forall d\ P(k, d, t)$
options.why: That needs a trader on each desk with four profits. Every trader has a loss.

feedback.correct: Right. $\forall k\ \exists d\ \forall t$ and $\forall k\ \forall d\ \exists t$ are true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each claim, say what a witness must be, then check the table.

explain.text: Desks A and B have witness days Wednesday and Tuesday. On every day each desk has a profitable trader. No column is all profits, and every trader has a losing day.

items.title: Why the contrapositive agrees
items.prose: Put the steps of the argument in order. Two lines do not belong.
items.question: Order the steps that show $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$ agree.

lines.text: List the four rows of $P$ and $Q$: T, T; T, F; F, T; F, F
$P \Rightarrow Q$ reads T, F, T, T, since it fails only when $P$ is T and $Q$ is F
On each row, write $\lnot Q$ and $\lnot P$ by flipping $Q$ and $P$
$\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$ reads T, F, T, T: it fails only on the T, F row, where $\lnot Q$ is T and $\lnot P$ is F
The two columns agree on all four rows, so the statements are true in exactly the same cases
On the T, T row both are T, so they agree on every row
lines.why: One row is not all rows. The converse also agrees on the T, T row, yet it differs elsewhere.

lines.text: $Q \Rightarrow P$ reads T, T, F, T, which matches the original
lines.why: That is the converse, and it does not match: it differs on the T, F and F, T rows.

feedback.correct: Rows, both columns, then a row-by-row comparison.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the rows, compute both columns, then compare every row.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the argument needs. Both columns must be computed before you compare.
byKey.s5: The conclusion comes last, after both columns are known.
byKey.s1: Start by listing the four rows.

explain.text: Both columns are worked out on all four rows. They agree everywhere, so neither can be true where the other is false. Checking one row, or the converse, proves nothing.

items.title: Negating a limit
items.prose: Negate $\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon$ one step at a time. Each line gives its reason. Three lines are flawed.
items.question: Put the correct lines in order and leave the flawed ones out.

lines.text: $\lnot\big(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon\big)$, the statement to negate
$\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \lnot\big(\exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon\big)$, since not every $\varepsilon$ works means some $\varepsilon$ fails
$\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \lnot\big(\forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon\big)$, since no $N$ works means every $N$ fails
$\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n > N\ \lnot\big(|u_n - L| < \varepsilon\big)$, since not every $n > N$ works means some $n > N$ fails
$\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n > N,\ |u_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$, since not less than means at least
$\exists \varepsilon \le 0\ \lnot\big(\exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon\big)$, since the negation flips $\varepsilon > 0$ too
lines.why: The condition $\varepsilon > 0$ says which $\varepsilon$ we range over. Passing $\lnot$ flips the quantifier and keeps its domain.

lines.text: $\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$, negating the inequality only
lines.why: That leaves all three quantifiers as they were. Each one must flip as $\lnot$ passes it.

lines.text: $\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n > N,\ |u_n - L| > \varepsilon$, since not less than means greater than
lines.why: That drops the case $|u_n - L| = \varepsilon$. Not less than means greater than or equal to.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $\lnot$ past one quantifier per line, then negate the inequality.

byKey.left-out: You left out a correct step. Each quantifier needs its own line.

explain.text: Each line moves $\lnot$ past one quantifier and flips it, keeping its condition. The last line negates the inequality, with equality included. The result says that for some $\varepsilon$, however late we start, a later term lies at least $\varepsilon$ from $L$.

items.title: Only if
items.prose: A clearing house rule: **a trade settles only if both sides confirm it**.
items.question: Which statement says the same thing?

options.text: If either side does not confirm, the trade does not settle
If both sides confirm, the trade settles
options.why: You read “only if” as “if”. Confirmation may be needed without being enough.

options.text: If the trade does not settle, some side did not confirm
options.why: That is the converse's contrapositive. It may differ from the rule.

options.text: The trade settles exactly when both sides confirm
options.why: That adds a direction the rule does not state.

feedback.correct: Right. Settles $\Rightarrow$ both confirm, and its contrapositive is this.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write “$P$ only if $Q$” as $P \Rightarrow Q$, then take its contrapositive.

explain.text: The rule is “settles $\Rightarrow$ both confirm”. Its contrapositive is “not both confirm $\Rightarrow$ not settled”. By De Morgan, “not both confirm” is “either side does not confirm”.

items.title: A rule in a risk manual
items.prompt:
A risk manual says: **if the VIX closes above 30, every desk halves its position by the next close**. Read “halves” as “cuts to at most half”.

(a) Write the rule with quantifiers over days $d$ and desks $k$. Use $V(d)$ for “the VIX closes above 30 on day $d$”. Use $H(k, d)$ for “desk $k$ has halved its position by the close after day $d$”.

(b) Write its negation, moving $\lnot$ all the way in. Say in words what a breach looks like.

(c) Write the converse and the contrapositive, in symbols and in words.

(d) Say which of the converse and the contrapositive means the same as the rule, and why.

(e) Describe one record that would prove the rule was breached.
items.model:
**(a)** For every day, if the VIX closed above 30, then every desk halved:

$$\forall d\ \big(V(d) \Rightarrow \forall k\ H(k, d)\big)$$

**(b)** Negate one step at a time. $\lnot \forall d$ becomes $\exists d\ \lnot$. Then $\lnot(A \Rightarrow B)$ is $A \land \lnot B$. Then $\lnot \forall k$ becomes $\exists k\ \lnot$:

$$\exists d\ \big(V(d) \land \exists k\ \lnot H(k, d)\big)$$

In words: on some day the VIX closed above 30, yet some desk had not halved by the next close.

**(c)** Converse: $\forall d\ \big(\forall k\ H(k, d) \Rightarrow V(d)\big)$. Whenever every desk halved by the next close, the VIX had closed above 30.

Contrapositive: $\forall d\ \big(\exists k\ \lnot H(k, d) \Rightarrow \lnot V(d)\big)$. If some desk did not halve by the next close, the VIX did not close above 30 that day. Here $\lnot \forall k\ H$ became $\exists k\ \lnot H$.

**(d)** The contrapositive means the same as the rule. For each day, $A \Rightarrow B$ and $\lnot B \Rightarrow \lnot A$ have the same truth table: both fail only when $A$ is true and $B$ false. The converse can fail when the rule holds: every desk might halve on a calm day for its own reasons.

**(e)** One record is enough, because the negation is an $\exists$ claim. For example: on 5 March the VIX closed at 32.4. The rates desk held £40m at that close and £25m at the next. £25m is more than half of £40m, so that desk did not halve, and the rule was breached.

rubric.text: Writes $\forall d\ (V(d) \Rightarrow \forall k\ H(k, d))$, with $\forall k$ inside the conclusion.
Negates to $\exists d\ (V(d) \land \exists k\ \lnot H(k, d))$, flipping both quantifiers and turning the implication into an **and**, and says it in words.
Gives the converse and the contrapositive correctly, with $\lnot \forall k$ written as $\exists k\ \lnot$ in the contrapositive.
Says the contrapositive means the same, with a reason (same truth table), and that the converse does not.
Describes one record: a VIX close above 30 and a desk above half its position at the next close, with figures.
